sentence_as_it_stands: Days of skin anaesthesia from lecithin-coated methoxyflurane microdroplets. Four to eight days of human skin anaesthesia, from a 1991 paper read as an abstract only. It is the only human formulation that has ever produced days rather than hours of skin block. It was never developed, nothing in the sustained-release class since comes close, and nobody has looked at why it stopped.
quote: Both LIQ865 formulations demonstrated dose-dependent hypoesthesia and hypoalgesia. The duration of analgesia ranged between 37 and 86 h.
corrected_wording: Days of skin anaesthesia from lecithin-coated methoxyflurane microdroplets. Four to eight days of human skin anaesthesia, from a 1991 paper read as an abstract only. Other sustained-release formulations have since produced skin analgesia lasting days from a single dose in humans: liposomal bupivacaine intradermally for up to two days (Grant 2004, PMID 15220782), bupivacaine microcapsules subcutaneously for at least four days (Pedersen 2004, PMID 15333431) and PLGA microparticle bupivacaine subcutaneously for one and a half to three and a half days (Jensen 2024, PMID 38482995). The methoxyflurane formulation was never developed, and nobody has looked at why it stopped.
notes: Rests on Jensen 2024, which came from Rames' reference list (ref 5); quote from its cached abstract (cache redacted only for the toxicity passage). Same idea as claim C043 on 'The intradermal wheal literature nobody cites…', already refuted by the main session on Grant 2004 and the microcapsule studies; this is its second location, on the open-question page. The record contradicts itself here: 'Injectables ruled out but not tried' (section 'The rest of the class') records the microcapsules' effects 'for at least 96 hours' and LIQ865's '37 to 86 hours', and Grant 2004's 19 to 48 hours intradermally. sentence_as_it_stands: Injecting [dose figure omitted] articaine directly into a rat’s sciatic nerve left conduction measurably reduced three weeks later, with thinner fibers and thinner insulating sheaths; [dose figure omitted] did not produce those changes, and a needle plus salt water produced no effect at all (Hillerup et al., 2011).
quote: The evoked spinal cord field potential in the articaine groups faded away immediately after injection and was concentration-dependently, significantly more reduced at the 3-week follow-up in comparison with the saline group.
corrected_wording: Injecting articaine directly into a rat’s sciatic nerve left conduction reduced three weeks later in the articaine groups compared with salt water, more at the higher concentration; thinner fibers and thinner insulating sheaths were significant only at the higher concentration, and a needle plus salt water produced no effect at all (Hillerup et al., 2011).
notes: Came from Baroni's reference list (ref 28). Rests on the abstract only: it reports the three-week reduction for 'the articaine groups' against saline, concentration-dependently, and the fibre-area and myelin changes only for the higher concentration; it does not state the lower-concentration-versus-saline conduction test separately, so the full text should confirm (not reachable here: no PMC copy, and the Scite connector needs a paid plan). The record's articaine-wheals page reads the abstract the same way as this correction ('At three weeks, the response was still significantly more reduced than in the salt-water group, and the size of that reduction depended on concentration'), so the two pages disagree. Second place on this page: Sources, 'Damage to nerve tissue', Hillerup entry: 'Lasting conduction loss and structural change at [dose figure omitted] but not [dose figure omitted], with no effect from needle plus saline.'

section: What do the reports from dental practice show?
sentence_as_it_stands: The one systematic attempt to settle the question came out undecided.
quote: In this contribution, a literature review of possible neurotoxicity after use of articaine is described. … PubMed and Web of Science were searched with the search query described below.
corrected_wording: At least two systematic attempts to settle the question have come out undecided: Hopman and colleagues (2017) searched PubMed and Web of Science for clinical and laboratory studies of articaine and paraesthesia and concluded that further investigation was needed, and Stirrup and Crean (2019) searched for studies comparing nerve damage after articaine and lidocaine in lower-jaw nerve blocks and found seven.
notes: Same error in a second place: Sources — Reports from dental practice, Stirrup & Crean entry: 'The only systematic attempt to answer the question, and it comes out undecided'. Repeats claim update C057 (narrowed -> refuted on Hopman 2017) and adds both page locations. Hopman 2017 (Br Dent J, PMID 28972589, DOI 10.1038/sj.bdj.2017.782): two-database search with a PRISMA flow, 47 full texts read by two authors, 16 clinical and 4 laboratory studies; ends 'Further investigation of possible causes of paraesthesia after use of local anaesthetics seems to be warranted' (PDF p5). It calls itself a literature review and has no risk-of-bias assessment or meta-analysis. The page does not cite Hopman anywhere.

section: What does the laboratory say about damage to nerve cells?
sentence_as_it_stands: It does mean the single most favourable published fact about articaine's safety was produced by the company that sells it, and it should be weighted accordingly.
quote: Neuroblastoma cells have been incubated with different anaesthetics for 24 hours, and subsequent cell death was determined. … articaine proved to be less toxic than the other evaluated anaesthetics: tetracaine, bupivacaine, prilocaine, mepivacaine, ropivacaine and lidocaine.
corrected_wording: The first author of that study works for Septodont, which makes articaine and sells it in Mexico. The favourable laboratory ranking does not rest on that study alone: an independent university group had already found the same direction in two cell lines — articaine, equal with procaine, the least toxic of eight anaesthetics on human neuroblastoma cells over 24 hours (Werdehausen 2009), and second least toxic on T-lymphoma cells (Werdehausen 2012).
notes: Hopman 2017 (refs 27 and 28) reports both Werdehausen studies; their abstracts (PMIDs 19700777, 22012177, cached) confirm the orderings, with no manufacturer affiliation (Düsseldorf university anaesthesiology). Same point in a second place: Sources — Damage to nerve tissue, Malet entry ('the most favourable published safety fact about the drug comes from its maker'). Related: 'A second cell-line study compared the drugs as they come out of the cartridge' (Albalawi 2018) reads as if Malet and Albalawi were the only cell-line studies of articaine; Werdehausen 2009 and 2012 are two more. The record already describes both Werdehausen papers accurately on 'Injectables ruled out but not tried' (tetracaine section). The comparison page's 'The dish ranking also comes with an interest' is accurate as worded (it is about the study behind its table) and is not a finding. None of this bears on articaine injected inside a nerve (Hillerup 2011).

section: What do the reports from dental practice show?
sentence_as_it_stands: Haas and Lennon reviewed 21 years of reports from dentists in Ontario, Canada. The overall risk of paresthesia after a local anesthetic injection was about 1 in 785,000 injections.
quote: The market share of the local anaesthetics during the last year of the studied period was examined by the use of a questionnaire. Fourteen cases of paraesthesia were reported in 1993.
corrected_wording: Haas and Lennon reviewed 21 years of reports from dentists in Ontario, Canada (143 reports, 1973 to 1993), but their rates come from the final year alone: the 14 reports of 1993, all after articaine or prilocaine, projected against a survey of that year's anaesthetic use.
notes: The 1-in-785,000 figure in the sentence is an event incidence, not a dose figure, so it is kept verbatim. Haas & Lennon's own abstract (PMID 7736335, cached) says the same: 'In 1993 alone, there were 14 reports of paresthesia not associated with surgery. This can be projected to an incidence of' the figure the page quotes, and 'Articaine was administered in 10 of these cases or prilocaine in the other four.' Low because the page puts the 21-year review and the rate in adjacent sentences without stating that the rate came from it. The per-drug rates that follow on the page: the articaine figure matches Hopman's Table 1 for 1993; the figure for the lower-concentration solutions cannot come from the 1993 projection, since no 1993 report involved them, and neither Hopman nor the abstract shows where it comes from — unverified. The same framing appears more explicitly on prilocaine-wheals (F09).

section: Sources — Reports from dental practice (Piccinni C and colleagues)
sentence_as_it_stands: Among all local anesthetics, only articaine and prilocaine produced a paraesthesia signal, strongest in dentistry. Limits: as above.
quote: Adverse reactions were not related to market share, but a reporting odds ratio was calculated for each anaesthetic. This is the ratio between the cases of paraesthesia, and the number of other adverse reactions reported for the same anaesthetic.
corrected_wording: Among all local anesthetics, only articaine and prilocaine produced a paraesthesia signal, strongest in dentistry. Limits: voluntary reports; a case/non-case analysis that sets paraesthesia reports against all other reports for the same drug rather than against sales, so a drug that draws few other adverse-event reports shows a higher ratio — a point Hopman 2017 raises for articaine.
notes: 'Limits: as above' refers to the Garisto entry directly above it: 'voluntary reports compared against sales, which cannot separate events from reporting behaviour'. Piccinni's abstract (PMID 25420896, cached) confirms the case/non-case design with reporting odds ratios and no sales comparison. Hopman (PDF p4) adds that the authors 'did not seem to realise articaine's lower risk of systemic toxicity', which 'may also be (partly) responsible for the increased reporting odds ratio'; Hopman (PDF p5) also notes that Garisto and Piccinni searched the same database with different queries and found very different case counts. Low because 'as above' could be read as 'voluntary reports' only. The prilocaine-wheals page describes Piccinni's design correctly ('spontaneous reports with no denominator').

section: What happens when articaine is injected into a nerve?
sentence_as_it_stands: Later reviews describe it accurately and draw the obvious conclusion from it — that anesthetic concentration should be kept as low as the job allows.
quote: Articaine could, because of its different chemical structure with a thiophene ring, have a higher intrinsic neurotoxicity than other anaesthetics at equal concentrations. However, animal and in vitro investigations do not support this suggestion.
corrected_wording: Reviews that cite it describe it accurately. At least one later review of articaine neurotoxicity does not cite it at all (Hopman 2017): that review concludes from other animal and cell-culture studies that articaine is not more toxic than other amide anaesthetics, and names articaine's higher concentration as a possible explanation of its over-representation in paraesthesia reports.
notes: Adjacent to the C050 sentence ('Twenty-nine papers have cited it … None of them contradicts it'); the claim update for C050 records that Hopman 2017 is not a citing paper (its only Hillerup reference is Hillerup, Jensen & Ersbøll 2011, PMID 21531935, not the rat study PMID 21467556). This finding concerns the next sentence: read as 'reviews that cite it', it is accurate; read as 'later reviews of the subject', it leaves out a dedicated 2017 review that omits the rat study and reads the animal and cell-culture evidence the other way — hence low. Hopman's animal/in-vitro section covers Ribeiro 2003, Werdehausen 2009 and 2012, Malet 2015 and Baroni 2013 (PDF pp4-5).

section: 6.8a Four adjacent literatures on repeated or prolonged exposure — 1. Dental repeated injection
sentence_as_it_stands: `ABSTRACT-ONLY` Dentistry injects local anaesthetic into small tissue volumes repeatedly over decades. Pogrel 2000, Hillerup 2011 and Gaffen & Haas 2009 establish that **persistent paraesthesia after dental blocks is real but rare**, with **articaine and prilocaine disproportionately implicated**, and an unresolved debate over whether the cause is needle trauma or the neurotoxicity of concentrated agent.
quote: Persistent sensibility disorders after administration of local anaesthetics are rare. Several retrospective studies suggest a higher risk of paraesthesia after administration of articaine in a concentration of [dose figure omitted] compared to other anaesthetics used at lower concentrations.
corrected_wording: Pogrel 2000, Hillerup, Jensen and Ersbøll 2011 and Gaffen and Haas 2009 report that persistent paraesthesia after dental blocks is real but rare, with articaine and prilocaine disproportionately implicated, and an unresolved debate over whether the cause is needle trauma or the neurotoxicity of concentrated agent — a summary a full-text review of these and the other dental reporting studies bears out (Hopman 2017).
notes: Verification is secondary: Hopman 2017 reviews all three sources (refs 6, 21, 15; PMIDs 10916328, 21531935, 19840499) in full text — persistent sensory disorders rare (PDF p5), articaine over-represented in most reporting studies and prilocaine at its higher strength too (PDF pp3, 5), and the needle-versus-neurotoxicity dispute set out on PDF p5 ('This suggestion is rejected by Hillerup and colleagues'). The page gives no full citation for 'Hillerup 2011'; in this dental-paraesthesia context it should be Hillerup, Jensen & Ersbøll 2011 (J Am Dent Assoc, PMID 21531935), not the rat sciatic-nerve study of the same year (PMID 21467556) that other pages cite — worth making explicit. Page tested by S1; findings only.

section: 6.8a Four adjacent literatures on repeated or prolonged exposure — 1. Dental repeated injection
sentence_as_it_stands: **1. Dental repeated injection — the closest thing to a repeated same-site human record.** … `INFERENCE` Relevant because it is the only body of human evidence on cumulative local anaesthetic exposure at a site — but it concerns **nerve-trunk blocks with [dose figure omitted] solutions**, not dermal wheals, and it never measures fibre density.
quote: Retrospective studies and clinical trials were included if they reported an incidence rate of paraesthesia or they evaluated the frequency of paraesthesia in relation to the market share of anaesthetics.
corrected_wording: The dental paraesthesia literature counts reported nerve injuries after individual injections, overwhelmingly single mandibular nerve blocks, against each drug's share of use; none of the reporting studies reviewed by Hopman 2017 records or analyses how many injections a person had received at a site, so it is human evidence on rare injury from single dental blocks, not on cumulative exposure at a site — and it concerns nerve-trunk blocks, not dermal wheals, and never measures fibre density.
notes: Hopman's inclusion rule (PDF p2) and every study description (PDF pp3-4: e.g. 'Every reported case of prolonged anaesthesia after the administration of a local anaesthetic was investigated'; cases attributed to a mandibular block, a mental nerve block or an infiltration) show per-injection case counting; no study in the review relates paraesthesia to repeated or cumulative injections. The only repeated-use item in Hopman is a Dutch court case about systemic complaints (Box 1), not a study. The page labels the sentence an inference; low because it is wording that overreaches rather than a figure. Page tested by S1; findings only.

page: 2 — Reference — Topical Treatments for Small Fiber Neuropathy
section: 4.9.3 · Ropivacaine and articaine injectables
sentence_as_it_stands: **Articaine carries the field’s one clinical argument that concentration itself is neurotoxic.**
quote: This suggestion is supported by the observation that prilocaine used in a concentration of [dose figure omitted], is also associated with an increased incidence of paraesthesia,13,17 while used in a concentration of [dose figure omitted] the opposite was found.
corrected_wording: Articaine does not carry the clinical argument that concentration itself is neurotoxic alone: in the dental reporting data the over-representation of articaine, sold at a higher concentration than most dental anaesthetics, is matched by prilocaine at its higher marketed strength, while prilocaine at a lower strength was under-represented in the Danish registry (Hopman 2017, reviewing Haas and Lennon 1995, Pogrel 2012 and Hillerup, Jensen and Ersbøll 2011).
notes: Hopman's Discussion (PDF p5) makes the concentration argument from both drugs: articaine's higher concentration as 'A possible explanation', supported by the prilocaine strength contrast (refs 13, 17 = Haas & Lennon 1995, Pogrel 2012; ref 21 = Hillerup, Jensen & Ersbøll 2011). Garisto 2010, which the record cites elsewhere, also found the higher-strength prilocaine over-represented. Only the first sentence of the Reference paragraph is reproduced; the rest of that paragraph (a trial, an umbrella review and a concentration recommendation) and the section's dose lines are left out under the filter rule. The Reference does not cite Hopman.

section: Sources — Nerve irritation and nerve damage (Haas DA, Lennon D entry); also 'What does the evidence say about prilocaine irritating nerves?'
sentence_as_it_stands: Limits: voluntary reports over 21 years divided by estimated injection counts, so both numerator and denominator are approximate; and the rates are for dental injections, overwhelmingly lower-jaw nerve blocks.
quote: The market share of the local anaesthetics during the last year of the studied period was examined by the use of a questionnaire. Fourteen cases of paraesthesia were reported in 1993.
corrected_wording: Limits: the rates are projections from the 14 reports of 1993 alone (four of them after prilocaine, the rest after articaine), set against a survey of that year's anaesthetic use — not 21 years of reports divided by injection counts; voluntary reports, and overwhelmingly lower-jaw nerve blocks.
notes: Second location on the same page, in 'What does the evidence say about prilocaine irritating nerves?': 'An earlier review of 21 years of Canadian reports put the absolute rates in perspective: about 1 in [dose figure omitted] overall, about 1 in 1,250,000 for the 2 and [dose figure omitted] solutions, and about 1 in 588,000 for [dose figure omitted] prilocaine (Haas and Lennon, 1995).' (the first masked figure is the 1-in-785,000 incidence). Haas & Lennon's abstract (PMID 7736335, cached) confirms the 1993-only basis: 14 reports in 1993, articaine in 10 and prilocaine in the other four; Hopman (PDF p3) gives prilocaine 28% of the 1993 cases against a 20% market share. Because no 1993 report involved the lower-concentration solutions, the 1-in-1,250,000 figure the page gives for them cannot come from that projection; neither Hopman nor the abstract shows its basis (unverified). Medium because the Sources entry states the basis explicitly and wrongly; the same framing, less explicit, is F03 on articaine-wheals.

section: What does the evidence say about prilocaine irritating nerves?
sentence_as_it_stands: **On the unfavourable side: the [dose figure omitted] dental solution carries the strongest paresthesia signal of any local anesthetic.**
quote: Articaine was used in 71% of these cases, while its market share was 38%. … Prilocaine [dose figure omitted] was also associated with a slightly increased incidence of paraesthesia
corrected_wording: On the unfavourable side: the higher-strength dental solution carries one of the two strongest paresthesia signals of any local anesthetic; whether prilocaine or articaine leads depends on the dataset — prilocaine in the US sales-adjusted reports (Garisto 2010) and a Californian referral series (Pogrel 2012), articaine in Ontario's 1993 reports (Haas and Lennon 1995) and in the US reporting-odds analysis (Piccinni 2015).
notes: Hopman 2017 (PDF p3) on Haas & Lennon's 1993 data: articaine 71% of cases against a 38% market share, prilocaine at its higher strength 28% against 20% ('slightly increased'); on Pogrel 2012: prilocaine at its higher strength in 34% of cases with an 8% market share, articaine not over-represented. The page itself already notes that Piccinni's ordering is the reverse of Garisto's and says to hold the figures loosely, so the overstatement is in the bolded headline only — hence low.

section: The ester question
sentence_as_it_stands: The amides — lidocaine, mepivacaine, bupivacaine, ropivacaine, prilocaine, articaine — are joined by an amide bond instead, are not cut in plasma, and are cleared by the liver.
quote: The amide structure of articaine is similar to that of other local anaesthetics, but it contains an additional ester group which is quickly hydrolysed by esterases. … since blood and serum are the sites of metabolism.
corrected_wording: The amides — lidocaine, mepivacaine, bupivacaine, ropivacaine, prilocaine — are joined by an amide bond instead, are not cut in plasma, and are cleared by the liver; articaine is an amide that also carries an ester group, which esterases in the blood hydrolyse quickly (Oertel 1997).
notes: Rests on an extra study from Hopman 2017's reference list: Oertel, Rahn & Kirch 1997 (Clin Pharmacokinet, PMID 9435991, Hopman ref 19; abstract cached with its dose, plasma-level and toxicity passages redacted). Hopman itself states only that articaine's thiophene ring 'also contains an additional ester group' (PDF p1). The articaine-wheals page already gets this right ('the ester side chain that lets blood enzymes destroy it'), so this is a cross-page inconsistency; low because articaine is not the subject of the Procaine page.
